beats.text: You settled too early. Or you waited too long. There's a rule for that!
Say you'll date ten people, one after another. Once you pass on someone, they're gone. So when do you commit?
The math says: skip the first thirty-seven percent. Just look. Then pick the first one who beats them all.
Let's simulate a thousand love lives. Ten dates each. Here's how often each strategy found the very best one.

beats.text: The rule: forty percent! Committing to the first date, or picking at random: only about ten.
Real life is messier. People can say no, and you never know how many you'll meet.
But the lesson holds: explore first. Then commit.

ask: TOO EARLY OR TOO LATE? COMMENT.
sources: Ferguson (1989), Who solved the secretary problem?, Statistical Science 4(3), 282–289 – optimal stopping: reject the first n/e (~37%) candidates, then take the first who beats all of them; the probability of picking the best approaches 1/e ≈ 37% (for n = 10: skip 3, ≈ 39.9%).
Christian & Griffiths (2016), Algorithms to Live By – application of the 37% rule to dating.
Simulation in this video: 1,000 runs, 10 candidates with random quality; the skip-3 rule found the best 401 times; first date 90 times; random choice 107 times.
